brief.headline: Push for ₹28.69 L saving by matching Mars Plastics & Premier Plastic prices on key SKUs, then offer 30-day payment for a further discount tied to their 4.54% borrowing rate.

priceAsk.summary: Cut prices on top three SKUs to match Mars Plastics and Premier Plastic; save ₹28.69 L/year total.
priceAsk.target: PP cap: ₹0.81/NOS (Mars price), HDPE bottle: ₹1.38/NOS (Mars price), measuring cup: ₹0.35/NOS (Premier price)
priceAsk.basis: We pay Mars ₹0.81 for the same PP cap while Cincorp charges ₹1.08 (33.2% gap, costing us ₹14.05 L extra). HDPE bottle gap is 10.7% (₹7.88 L extra), measuring cup gap is 30.6% (₹6.75 L extra). Open-market asks for the 28 mm cap sit at ₹0.55–1.20/pc (typical ₹0.85–0.95), so our ₹0.81 Mars price is market-fair and Cincorp's ₹1.08 sits at the high end—room to come down.

paymentTermAsk.summary: Move from 45 days to 30 days, and ask for a price cut of about 4.5% in return.
paymentTermAsk.cashImpact: Frees up ₹16.02 L cash for us if we move to 30 days (though we give back 15 days, the cut offsets it).

brief.financialLeverage: Cincorp is small—₹4.11 Cr revenue—and we're 47.43% of their business, so losing us would hurt. They keep only 6.0% of every ₹100 they sell, well below similar firms' 15.0%, meaning profit is tight and a deep price cut will sting. They owe 1.13 times their own cash and borrow money at about 4.54%, so cash matters to them; offering to pay 15 days faster is worth that rate, roughly 4–5%, which buys us negotiating room. Their cash is tied up for 101 days (close to the 107-day peer norm), and they already pay their own suppliers slower (39 days vs 23 for peers), so we can fairly ask them to absorb faster payment from us. Push firmly on price to close the ₹28.69 L gap, then trade payment speed for an extra few percent off—but don't squeeze so hard you destabilize a supplier who makes half their revenue from you.

evidence.point: We're paying ₹28.69 L/year more than the cheapest prices we already get
PP cap costs us ₹1.08/NOS here, but Mars delivers it at ₹0.81/NOS—a 33.2% gap costing ₹14.05 L/year
We are 47.43% of their total ₹4.11 Cr revenue
They keep 6.0% profit, much less than peers' 15.0%—so margins are thin
They borrow at about 4.54%, meaning 15-day faster payment is worth roughly that rate to them
Paying 30 days instead of 45 frees ₹16.02 L cash for us

alternates.name: Manjushree Technopack Ltd
alternates.why: India's largest rigid-plastic packaging converter (₹2569.83 Cr revenue, health B 65/100)—makes pharma bottles, caps, preforms; a proven, strong second source.

alternates.name: Mold-Tek Packaging Ltd
alternates.why: Listed rigid-plastic leader (₹1010.97 Cr revenue, health B 73/100) with pharma capability—robust alternate for bottles and closures.

risks: They're a small supplier (₹4.11 Cr, health C 51/100) and we're nearly half their business—pushing too hard on price could destabilize them or push them to walk away.
Their profit is only 6.0% (peers: 15.0%), so a big price cut bites harder here than at a healthier supplier; balance the ask with faster payment to sweeten the deal.
They owe 1.13 times their own cash; supply risk is modest (they cover interest 4.77 times over) but watch for any payment delays or quality slips that signal trouble.
Altman Z-score of 1.83 puts them in the grey zone—not in distress, but not rock-solid either; have Manjushree or Mold-Tek ready as a backup before you press the final discount.
brief.suggestedOpeningLine: We value the partnership, but right now we're paying ₹28.69 lakh more per year than our best prices on the same items—let's work together to close that gap and talk about how faster payment from us can help your cash flow.
